newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori denies troops executed rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori denies troops executed rebels.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori on Friday denied reports that his troops had executed some of the 14 Marxist rebels slain in the assault on the Japanese ambassador's residence.

"That is completely false. There were no executions," Fujimori told Reuters in his first interview since Tuesday's daring military strike that freed alive all but one of the 72 hostages, ending the four-month siege.

He said five of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels died in the initial explosion as soldiers blasted into the residence, while five others including leader Nestor Cerpa died rushing up a staircase. The other four lost their lives while fighting troops in the upper story, he said.
Various military, intelligence and hostage sources have said two guerrillas were shot after being captured and that at least one more begged to surrender.

Asked if the troops had an order to kill and take no prisoners, Fujimori replied: "The order and the objective was to free the 72 hostages, not one less. We achieved freeing 72 with one who died afterwards."

Fujimori, speaking in the presidential palace, said the operation was intended to last six minutes but it was complicated by a stubborn, 16-minute resistance by MRTA fighters in the house's northern wing.

A relaxed and smiling Fujimori praised the "Peruvian creativity" that went into the three months of preparation for the raid. Sixty men worked 24 hours a day, shifting 200 truckloads of earth and employing "an incredible amount of wood" to construct 190 yards (metres) of tunnels underneath the residence, he said.
Elite troops swarmed into the residence on Tuesday afternoon through the tunnels.

Although he would not give details of the electronic devices used to warn hostages of the assault, he revealed that periscopes were used to spy on the rebels and help choose the moment when the troops entered -- as MRTA members were playing indoor soccer.
"I am very proud," he said, praising his intelligence services and armed forces.

Fujimori pledged to try to "eliminate all violence" in Peru and leave "no trace" of the MRTA or the larger Maoist guerrilla movement Shining Path. But, in contrast to his attitude after previous blows against the guerrillas, he was careful to avoid over-confidence after Tuesday's successful military operation.
He ruled out a political peace accord or a new amnesty law as tactics to pacify Peru. And he added that security forces were "alert" against threats of reprisal attacks from the MRTA.
